messages.subject: Multilevel confimatory factor analysis
parts:
Hello everyone,

I am trying to run a Multilevel confirmatory model, and I am using the following code:

##TWO LEVEL
twolevel <- '
level: 1
  aw =~ Amp_1 + Amp_2 + Amp_3
  ew =~ Exh_1 + Exh_2 +  Exh_3 + Exh_4 + Exh_5 + Exh_6 + Exh_7 + Exh_8 + Exh_9
  cw =~ Accom_1 + Accom_2 + Accom_3 + Accom_4 + Accom_5 + Accom_6 + Accom_7 + Accom_8
  dw =~ Dep_1 + Dep_2 + Dep_3 + Dep_4 + Dep_5
level: 2
  ab =~ Amp_1 + Amp_2 + Amp_3
  eb =~ Exh_1 + Exh_2 +  Exh_3 + Exh_4 + Exh_5 + Exh_6 + Exh_7 + Exh_8 + Exh_9
  cb =~ Accom_1 + Accom_2 + Accom_3 + Accom_4 + Accom_5 + Accom_6 + Accom_7 + Accom_8
  db =~ Dep_1 + Dep_2 + Dep_3 + Dep_4 + Dep_5'

Nevertheless, the output shows the following message:
WARNING: the optimizer warns that a solution has NOT been found! Warning: lavaan WARNING: estimation of the baseline model failed.
I am just starting to use this Model. Thus, what can I do to find a solution? Can anyone tell me where I can get information to solve this problem?
I really appreciate any help you can provide.
Kind Regards,

parts:
Much of what comes around on the list is way beyond me but I am learning a huge amount from this but for once
I think I can contribute. 

Why do you map from the number of variables to guide about sample size Jeremy?  To my mind this is a bad 
approach, "rules" like "n >= 4k"  and even "n >= 10k" (where k is number of items) went around back in pre-CFA
days (and still surface in EFA/PCA papers I see).  However, I thought that early simulation work like Guadagnoli
& Velicer (1988). Relation of sample size to the stability of component patterns. Psychological Bulletin, 103,
265–275 and Velicer & Fava (1998).  The effects of variable and subject sampling on factor pattern recovery.
Psychological Methods, 3, 231–251 showed that the relationship between desirable n and k was actually the 
reverse: the higher the k the smaller the n to recover known population factor/component structures, but that
the desirable n was much more a function of the number of factors in the population model and my recollection
is that one of the simulation papers of the time proposed n > 50 for single factor models and n > 40*p (where 
p was the number of factors, hope I'm not misremembering the way that work used "p" and "k" --- but I'm sure
I'm not misremembering the logic).  That always seemed sensible and again I'm sure one of the papers said
this: the more items you have per factor the more internal reliability in principle so more power for recovery of
the population model.  Back in those EFA days the other issues were that low loadings in the population model
of course increased desirable n, as did oblique rather than orthogonal factors and simple rather than cross-loaded
models.

If we pull that logic across the multilevel CFA isn't the desirable number of groups > 50 for a single factor model
and > 40p for a p factor model?  My guts say that a lot would depend on the what's happening within the groups
though and n = 450 and n(groups) = 25 gives some very, very small groups at the first level doesn't it?  That 
might worry as much as the number of groups ... but I haven't followed this thread carefully enough to
understand the data and the model: apologies!

Am I completely misreading this sample size issue?

Very best all and thanks for a wonderfully educational list,

Chris

messages.subject: Re: Multilevel confimatory factor analysis
parts:
On Sun, 9 Oct 2022 at 01:37, Chris Evans <ch...@psyctc.org> wrote:

[snip]

Why do you map from the number of variables to guide about sample size Jeremy?  To my mind this is a bad 
approach, "rules" like "n >= 4k"  and even "n >= 10k" (where k is number of items) went around back in pre-CFA
days (and still surface in EFA/PCA papers I see).

[snip]

Because the sample size in this case is so low that the covariance matrix will not be positive definite and therefore the model will not be identified and it is inevitable that this error will occur.

If I was asked by someone who was planning that study and devising their sampling plan what they should do, I'd guess about 100 as a starting point, but I'd spend a lot longer doing (things like) simulations to try to determine what was an adequate number. 

I'm not sure that the sample size in each group is an issue. I don't see why (but that might be my lack of knowledge / understanding) two individuals per group would be a problem.

[Lots of useful info that I agree with snipped in the name  of brevity, see previous email in thread].

Jeremy
